name: Benzedrine

lead: Benzedrine was the first pharmaceutical amphetamine, and amphetamine is classed as an anorectic, meaning it suppresses appetite. Its historical role in appearance culture is as a slimming drug: reduced appetite leads to eating less, which can lead to weight loss and a leaner look.

Today amphetamine sulfate is a prescription medicine for conditions such as ADHD and narcolepsy rather than a slimming product. Medical reviews describe its use for excessive daytime sleepiness and ADHD, and the 1938 British Medical Journal carried an article simply titled 'Benzedrine'.

paras: Historically it was taken by mouth as tablets prescribed by doctors. Today any use is under medical prescription for approved conditions; it is not marketed for weight loss in the way it once was.

Amphetamine is a US Schedule II substance, Canadian Schedule I and UK Class B. Reported effects include insomnia, mood swings, appetite loss, dry mouth and raised heart rate and blood pressure; heavy use can cause psychosis and serious dependence. Anyone considering it should rely on a prescriber.

chain: Weight loss and a leaner physique
angle.text: Historically prescribed so patients would eat less and slim down. Today it is a prescription stimulant, and its weight effects are incidental to its approved uses.

lead: Benzedrine was the brand name of the first amphetamine pharmaceutical, sold by Smith, Kline and French from 1933.[1][2] Amphetamine itself was first synthesized in 1887 by Lazar Edeleanu and entered drug use in the late 1920s.[1] The generic name of the sulfate form is amphetamine sulfate, still sold under brands such as Evekeo.[3]

Its link to looks is weight and body shape. Amphetamine suppresses appetite, and mid-twentieth-century physicians prescribed it as a slimming aid: eating less led to weight loss and a leaner figure. Wikipedia lists decreased appetite among its effects, lists obesity among the conditions Benzedrine sulfate was used to treat after its introduction around 1936, and describes amphetamine as having been sold commercially as an appetite suppressant.[1][2][4]

Research on amphetamine sulfate today concerns ADHD, sleepiness disorders and psychiatry.[5][6][7] The drug is tightly controlled in most countries, and amphetamine sulfate (Evekeo) remains among the amphetamine-type drugs FDA-approved for short-term obesity treatment.[1][4]
infobox: US Schedule II; Canada Schedule I; UK Class B

paras: Appetite suppression made Benzedrine a historical weight-loss drug.[1][4] The appearance goal for patients was a slimmer body through lower food intake, which is the same chain modern appetite-suppressant and weight-loss medicines rely on.[4]

Amphetamine sulfate is used for ADHD and for excessive daytime sleepiness, where stimulants including amphetamine sulfate are described as standard pharmacotherapy.[3][5][7] Historically it was also used for nasal congestion and depression.[2] A 1987 review looked at psychostimulants in general psychiatry half a century after the introduction of Benzedrine.[6]

Amphetamine was synthesized in 1887 by Lazar Edeleanu but had no medical use until the early 1930s.[1][2] The American pharmacologist Gordon Alles reported its physiological effects in 1928, treating it as a synthetic relative of ephedrine, and he later served as a consultant to Smith, Kline and French from 1934 to 1951, selling his patent rights to the company.[8]

In late 1933 Smith, Kline and French began selling amphetamine as a Benzedrine inhaler marketed as a decongestant; Benzedrine sulfate tablets followed about three years later.[2] The company's amphetamine line later included Dexedrine pills and Dexamyl tablets.[8] The medical press was discussing Benzedrine by 1938, when the British Medical Journal carried an article simply titled 'Benzedrine'.[9]

During World War II both Allied and Axis forces used amphetamine and methamphetamine extensively for alertness and performance, and Wikipedia states that the UK and US militaries supplied large numbers of Benzedrine tablets.[2][4] After the war, surplus amphetamines moved to civilian markets, where amphetamine was sold as an appetite suppressant, and Wikipedia states that safety concerns led to tight restrictions in most parts of the world from the late 1950s.[4] In the 1960s amphetamine became part of UK mod culture, where one historian argued users valued the 'smart, on-the-ball, cool image' it gave.[2]

Amphetamine is a central nervous system stimulant. Its effects at normal medical doses include alertness, appetite loss and raised heart rate and blood pressure.[1][2] Appetite suppression is the effect linked to reduced food intake and weight loss.[2]

Common effects include increased alertness, insomnia, mood swings, appetite loss, dry mouth and elevated heart rate or blood pressure. Heavy use can cause psychosis, high doses can cause rapid muscle breakdown, and addiction is a serious risk.[1] Wikipedia notes that dose is the main factor in how likely and severe side effects are, and that addiction is unlikely with long-term medical use at therapeutic doses.[2]

Amphetamine is a prescription drug in many countries: US Schedule II, Canadian Schedule I, UK and New Zealand Class B, Australian S8 and UN Psychotropic Schedule II.[1][2] The name Benzedrine survives mostly as a historical reference in literature, forums and popular history, where it is associated with wartime alertness, mid-century dieting and productivity, for example in T Nation threads that mention Benzedrine inhalers being legal until the 1950s.[10]

Other appetite suppressants have since been withdrawn for safety reasons, including aminorex in the 1960s, fenfluramine in the 1990s and phenylpropanolamine in 2000, which is part of the background to the heavily regulated status of stimulant weight-loss drugs.[4]

Trials of amphetamine sulfate focus on ADHD and other conditions,[5][7] and a review covers research into amphetamine for stroke recovery.[11] A review of ADHD trials from 1999-2021 lists amphetamine sulfate among the common stimulant drug classes studied.[7] A Medical Letter review covers racemic amphetamine sulfate (Evekeo) for ADHD.[3]
